title: HL extension: motivation and technology
summary: How motivation drives behaviour in learning and health, and how digital technology affects cognition, well-being, relationships and treatment.

keyterms.definition: Doing something because it is enjoyable or satisfying in itself.
Doing something to gain a reward or avoid a punishment.
Deci & Ryan: motivation thrives when needs for autonomy, competence and relatedness are met.
Expected external rewards for an enjoyable activity can reduce intrinsic motivation.
Prochaska & DiClemente: people move through stages of change, from precontemplation to maintenance.
People remember less information they expect to be able to look up, but remember where to find it.
Using several media at once, linked to poorer filtering of distractions.
Treating anxiety by exposing people to feared situations in virtual reality.
How technology use relates to mental health, mood and life satisfaction.

questions.prompt: Lepper, Greene and Nisbett (1973) told some preschoolers they would get a certificate for drawing. Later, these children:
options: Drew less in free time than children not expecting a reward
questions.explanation: An expected reward reduced intrinsic interest: the overjustification effect.

questions.prompt: Self-determination theory says motivation depends on needs for:
questions.explanation: Meeting these psychological needs supports intrinsic motivation.

questions.statement: Murayama and Kuhbandner (2011) found monetary rewards improved delayed memory for boring trivia but not for interesting trivia.
questions.explanation: Extrinsic rewards helped where intrinsic interest was low.

questions.statement: In the transtheoretical model, the first stage is action.
questions.explanation: It begins with precontemplation, then contemplation and preparation, before action and maintenance.

questions.text: The decline in intrinsic interest after expected rewards is the ___ effect.
questions.explanation: Rewards can shift the reason for an activity from enjoyment to payment.

questions.text: Doing homework only to avoid detention is ___ motivation.
questions.explanation: Extrinsic motivation comes from outside consequences.

questions.prompt: Match each concept to a context.
questions.explanation: Motivation is relevant across all four contexts.

questions.prompt: Adcock et al. (2006) found that cues signalling high reward before encoding led to better memory and activation in:
options: Reward-related midbrain areas and the hippocampus
questions.explanation: This links motivation (reward) to memory biologically.

questions.prompt: Which classroom change best supports autonomy according to SDT?
options: Giving students meaningful choices in how they complete tasks
questions.explanation: Choice supports autonomy and intrinsic motivation.

questions.prompt: Order the stages of the transtheoretical model.
questions.explanation: Interventions should match the stage a person is in.

questions.prompt: Sparrow, Liu and Wegner (2011) found that when people expected information to be saved on a computer they:
options: Remembered the information less but remembered where it was saved
questions.explanation: The internet may act as an external memory store: the "Google effect".

questions.prompt: Ophir, Nass and Wagner (2009) found heavy media multitaskers were:
options: Worse at filtering irrelevant information and task switching
questions.explanation: This is correlational: multitasking may cause poor filtering, or vice versa.

questions.statement: Mueller and Oppenheimer (2014) found students taking notes by laptop did worse on conceptual questions than those writing by hand.
questions.explanation: Laptop users tended to transcribe verbatim, processing material less deeply.

questions.statement: Hunt et al. (2018) found limiting social media use to about 10 minutes per platform per day increased loneliness.
questions.explanation: Limiting use reduced loneliness and depressive symptoms over three weeks.

questions.text: Przybylski and Weinstein (2017) proposed the "___ hypothesis": moderate screen use is not harmful.
questions.explanation: Very high use was linked to slightly lower well-being, but moderate use was not.

questions.text: Treating fear of heights by exposure to virtual heights is virtual reality ___ therapy.
questions.explanation: Rothbaum et al. (1995) found VR exposure reduced acrophobia compared with a waiting list.

questions.prompt: Match each study to its finding.

pairs.right: Expecting access reduces recall of facts
VR exposure reduced fear of heights

questions.explanation: Technology affects cognition, well-being and treatment.

questions.prompt: Why is it hard to establish that social media causes depression?
options: Most studies are correlational, and depressed people may use social media more
questions.explanation: Bidirectionality and third variables limit causal claims; experiments like Hunt et al. help.

questions.prompt: A strength of VR exposure therapy compared with real-life exposure is that:
options: Exposure can be controlled precisely and done safely in the clinic
questions.explanation: Therapists can control intensity step by step.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of VR exposure therapy for fear of heights.
items: Expose to the lowest virtual height
Move up the hierarchy as anxiety falls
questions.explanation: This mirrors systematic desensitization using technology.
